paper_title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which an AI system uses its own capabilities to build more capable successor [23, 57], is one of the proposed routes to superhuman intelligence [20]. Its early forms are already reported [2, 19]: AI systems write most of the code inside the companies that build them [8], and agents carry out growing share of the research [50]. For language models, the part of this loop open to study is post-training: pretraining establishes the knowledge foundation [24, 27, 33], while post-training shapes instruction following, reasoning, coding, and alignment [25, 35, 36, 49, 72]. Yet post-training research remains an expensive iterative search, and published reports typically document the final recipe rather than the full research trajectory that produced it [14, 22, 54, 73]. Search over data mixtures, objectives, algorithms, and hyperparameters is an evidence-driven loop that agents have begun to automate [13, 43, 48] and benchmarks have begun to evaluate [9, 44, 66]. We study autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain), where frontier agent diagnoses base models weaknesses, runs training experiments at scale, and iteratively refines its recipes from the evidence. Existing work studies narrower versions of this problem. PostTrainBench and Locus have agents train separate specialist for each benchmark [29, 55], and other benchmarks and systems isolate fine-tuning, reinforcement-learning engineering, data-centric research, or structured agent workflows [12, 17, 38, 46, 75]. These works also allow teacher models or do not keep held-out evaluation sealed from the agents. Our setting takes the harder choice on every one of these points: one generalist checkpoint must improve on six capabilities at once, starting from raw base model, with no teacher model, and it is scored on held-out suite that the agents never see, which tests the same capabilities on other questions. AutoPostTrain is expensive: one hypothesis can take hours of failure-prone GPU execution before its checkpoint can be evaluated. It is also hard to keep honest: search that runs for days must keep its training data clean and its final evaluation sealed [64, 69]. For an agent to do this research, experiments must be easy to 2 Figure 2 Athanor at glance. Each researcher agent works in its own sandbox on GPU node, with its own coding tools, and reaches the GPUs through one command: athanor job, eval, data, and artifact run jobs, request evaluations, bring in data, and save or submit checkpoints. The environment runs the jobs, decontaminates incoming data, scores checkpoints with frozen evaluator, and records every request and result for the team. The operator, who runs the campaign, sets it up, recovers lost nodes, and scores the teams submission on the held-out suite. submit, the evaluation must stay out of the agents reach, and, because the search outlasts any one session, the research state must be externalized : kept outside the agents context, with each result linked to the evidence then available and the recipe that produced it. We build Athanor (Figure 2), an open agent-native system that enables frontier agents to hill-climb raw base model through long-running campaigns of training experiments on real GPUs. Our design thesis is that, as agent intelligence improves, the bottleneck in autonomous research shifts from generating plausible ideas to the friction of executing and verifying them: without managed execution, an agent spends hours debugging training infrastructure and rebuilds the same machinery for every experiment. Athanor therefore makes post-training research programmable: it gives research its atomic operations (starting job, evaluating checkpoint, bringing in data), the agent composes them in its own code, and the environment carries them out. The system is agent-native in that the agent does research with its own coding and analysis tools. The central design question is how to empower agents, not imprison them: the agents keep every research decision, while experiment execution stays efficient, auditable, and recoverable. Three design principles make this work. First, separate research decisions from execution: the agent inspects data and model behavior, writes its own data and training programs, and decides what to run; the environment runs, measures, and recovers every experiment. Second, externalize the research state: every request, result, checkpoint lineage, transcript, and note stays in durable record, so session can be resumed or replaced, several agents can work as team [51], and every campaign can be audited. Third, keep the research loop productive: jobs run in the background and each result reaches the agent the moment it arrives, so an agent keeps several experiments in flight. We evaluate Athanor in large-scale post-training campaign. Four agents (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code [3]) form team, each on one node of eight GPUs, and start from Qwen3-4B-Base with public data, no teacher-model calls, and no research advice from humans. In 104 hours the team raises the base from 15.9 to 67.3 on six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on held-out suite of different questions for the 3 same capabilities, which the agents never know exists; the vendors Qwen3-4B-Instruct-25071 scores 66.5 and 47.9 under the same evaluator (Figure 1, Table 1). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first public result in which team of AI agents, working autonomously, post-trains raw base model into one cross-domain generalist model at the level of the vendors instruct release, confirmed on the held-out suite. Earlier results at this level come from human teams recipe, Tülu 3, which generated training data with stronger models [36], or from agents that train one specialist per benchmark or call teacher models [16, 29]; other agent systems report gains on tasks seen during development or on one task family [47, 61]. Section 7 and Appendix compare the agent systems. The vendor describes building its small Qwen3 models by distillation from its own larger flagship models [72]; the agents reach the same level from public data, much of which was itself distilled from stronger models by its publishers [1, 36, 73]. We then analyze the full record of the campaign, including the agents transcripts and notes, and find (Section 5): (1) recombination: the recipe chains known methods (supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, weight merging, and self-distillation), and the agents contribute the composition and the small changes that make it work; (2) team progress: ideas and checkpoints move between agents within hours, and every new best after hour 21 combines the training of several agents; (3) recipe convergence: within the first hour of the campaign, all four agents build on the same public corpus of reasoning traces, and the alternatives they try later score lower and are dropped; and (4) uneven data sense: the agents catch problems of format, length, scorability, and difficulty in their data but rarely check whether its answers are correct. Taken together, the agents engineering, planning, reasoning, and knowledge of post-training already suffice to take raw base model to the level of the vendors instruct release. Once the friction of execution is removed, the clearest limit we observe is how many different ideas they try: four copies of one agent model start from the same prior, converge on one recipe early, and test few alternatives. How the output of this research, the best checkpoint and the understanding of post-training behind it, grows with the compute the agents spend is what we call autoresearch scaling (Section 2). In summary, this paper makes three contributions: Athanor, an open agent-native system for post-training research on real GPUs, with frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, and research record that links every score to the recipe behind it. Instruct-level post-training by team of agents: in 104 hours, and for about $12,000 in all (GPU time at rental prices and the agents inference), four agents post-train Qwen3-4B-Base into one crossdomain generalist model that matches or surpasses the vendors instruct release (67.3 against 66.5 on the development suite and 48.2 against 47.9 on held-out suite), without teacher model. Four findings on how the agents do research, from the campaigns full record (500 jobs, 255 requested full evaluations, and the lineage of every checkpoint): they recombine known methods, progress as team, converge early on one recipe, and inspect the form of their data but rarely its correctness.

sections.title: 2.2 What Makes AutoPostTrain Hard
sections.content: In the RESEARCH step of (AutoPostTrain), the agent chooses Combinatorial, state-dependent search. recipe from high-dimensional, compositional space: discrete choices of data and method, continuous hyperparameters, and conditional training stages. Gradient descent optimizes parameters within stage; the researcher decides the order of training stages and their starting checkpoints. The choice is state-dependent: each stage trains the checkpoint produced by earlier stages, so upstream stages condition what later stages can achieve [79], and each new checkpoint enlarges the admissible set R(Pt). Since the benchmark scores that serve as feedback are not differentiable with respect to the recipe, the researcher can only propose promising recipe, observe noisy score, and keep the change if the score improves: the outer loop is stochastic black-box hill climbing [56]. What lets an agent do better than blind hill climber is its prior and the feedback it can reason over. researcher agents pretrained knowledge acts as strong scientific prior that concentrates proposals in small effective region of the recipe space, and it can reason about why change helped. To choose the next recipe within that region, it needs feedback it can act on. Because recipes effect depends on its starting checkpoint, each score is useful only if it is linked to the full lineage that produced it. Delayed, noisy, and incomplete feedback. The EXPERIMENT step of (AutoPostTrain) returns checkpoint and its full benchmark evaluation results. Post-training has no cheap proxy for this result: NanoGPT speedrunning can compare runs by common validation cross-entropy target [32], but post-training cannot, because its stages optimize losses on different scales, and even in pretraining, similar loss values can correspond to different downstream performance [11, 42]. To evaluate recipe, we must first train it, so there is delay τfb,t = τexec(rt) + τeval(M t, B), the time to prepare data and train plus the time to evaluate the checkpoint on B. The score is noisy: finite evaluation can blur the order of nearby candidates [45]. It is also incomplete: each benchmark covers only part of its capability, and IFEvals verifiable constraints, for example, cover only part of instruction following [83]. Scaling the research process. Pretraining scaling laws relate loss to compute for fixed training procedure [27, 33], and similar curves can be fit for RL post-training once the recipe is fixed [34]. If the recipe changes, no stable law is known that relates post-training compute to downstream performance. Here the recipe is what the agent searches for, so we ask how the output of the research grows as the agent completes more ), and the understanding of experiments and uses more compute: the best checkpoints capability c(M post-training that the experiments leave behind. We call this relationship autoresearch scaling. The process spends two resources: agent inference [50] pays for the analysis that invents new recipes, and training and evaluation compute turns those recipes into research artifacts, namely growing set of checkpoints and the scientific trajectory that produced them; Figures 1 and 4 show the capability curve against hours and cost, and Section 5 discusses why it flattens.

sections.title:
3.2 The Research Environment and Its Roles
The post-training research environment. We study a generalist setting in which one checkpoint must improve
across a suite of target capabilities, starting from a raw base model. Our environment gives each researcher a
coding workspace on a GPU node; a pool of public training corpora decontaminated against the benchmarks;
and the base model and the checkpoints saved by its team. Starter code, which the researcher may edit or
replace, covers building training datasets, supervised fine-tuning, group relative policy optimization (GRPO),
reinforcement learning in interactive environments, on-policy distillation from a team checkpoint, generating
logic puzzles, replaying public ALFWorld expert trajectories, and checkpoint merging, on the verl trainer [60]
and mergekit [21]. To test research ability under controlled conditions, the researcher cannot call or download
an external teacher model, and any further public dataset it brings in goes through the same decontamination
first. The evaluation is protected from the researchers. On request, the development suite returns every
benchmark score and every scored answer as feedback. A held-out suite, unknown to the researchers, gives
the result after the campaign.
sections.content: No human-designed research scaffolding. Athanor does not prescribe how the research is done. Following the bitter lesson [63], it builds no research procedure into the agent: the environment does not choose direction, approve an experiment, or interpret result, and the researchers run the harnesses that the model developers ship (Claude Code or Codex; this campaign uses Claude Code) through shell, files, and one command-line tool. In our experience, earlier versions of Athanor that prescribed form per recipe, an approval per experiment, and central scheduler constrained stronger agents more than they helped them. Others building agent systems report related effects: scaffolding written for weaker model can constrain the judgment of stronger one [81], and in one study prescribed roles made little difference to what agents produced [4]. What we improve between campaigns is therefore the environment, not research procedure: after each campaign we read the agents trajectories for points of friction, such as slow steps, confusing commands, and recurring workarounds, and improve the tools without changing the researchers role. Building Athanor is thus meta loop around the research loop. Researchers, environment, and operator. Athanor separates three roles by what each may decide and what each may see. The researchers make every research decision; they see their own and their teammates records and the development results, but not the held-out suite, and they cannot change the evaluator. Because the researchers are the ones being studied, these limits are enforced by the software: the sandbox, the frozen it runs what is evaluator, and the sealed held-out suite. The environment makes no research decision: 6 requested, measures with the frozen evaluator, and records what happened. The operator, person or an agent acting for one, has the widest authority and sees everything: it sets the campaigns goal and measurement protocol before the start, decides how long the campaign runs, keeps the nodes running, and scores the held-out suite. It gives no research advice, and every operator command leaves record.

sections.title: 3.3 Keeping the Loop Fast and Reliable
sections.content: In the terms of (AutoPostTrain), the researcher chooses rt and Separate research decisions from execution. the environment carries out Exec and Eval. The environment owns the tedious recurring work: resource allocation, job execution, checkpoint storage, evaluation, and recovery. This way the researchers effort goes into the research itself. The evaluator runs outside the researchers sandbox and grades by verifiable rules or programs, so its feedback follows fixed rules and stays beyond the reach of the researcher it measures. Externalize the research state. The research record is the history of (AutoPostTrain). It links each request to its code, data, and input checkpoints, and to the jobs, output checkpoints, and measurements that follow. It holds four kinds of entries. The journal is time-ordered log with one line for every accepted request and every change of state. The lineage records which checkpoints each checkpoint was made from. The transcript is the full text of every agent session. The workspace history is the version history of the workspace, including the researchers notes. Because every checkpoint points to its parents, we can trace any score back to the base model, through every training stage and merge that produced it. The record lives on storage outside the agents context, so researcher can resume session, start fresh one, or be moved to new node and still have the same evidence. For the same reason the researchers can work as team: each reads its teammates workspaces, results, and journals and can fetch their saved checkpoints. Keep the research loop productive. training job can take hours, and each of its checkpoints can be evaluated only once it is saved: training and evaluation together make up the feedback delay τfb of Section 2. researcher that waited for each result before starting the next experiment would leave most of its GPUs idle, so Athanor lets it keep several experiments in flight. Every job runs in the background and belongs to the environment rather than to the agents session: the agent can go on reading, planning, and starting other jobs, and the job survives if the session ends. When job or an evaluation finishes, the services push its result into the agents session, so one score can inform the next decision while other jobs are still running. Appendix gives the implementation of all three principles.

sections.title:
4.1 Experimental Setting
Agents and goal. Four researcher agents, each Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, work as one team; we
call them Agents 1–4. Each has one node, a sandbox, read-only web access, and the athanor command; a
node is a GPU server with eight GPUs, each with 80 GB of HBM3 memory, and a high-bandwidth GPU
interconnect. The goal they read is one sentence: raise the development-suite score of a model post-trained
from Qwen3-4B-Base as high as possible. It names no target score and prescribes no method. The agents see
the development scores of three reference models: the base, the default starter (the starter code run with its
default settings and no research), and Instruct-2507, so the level of the vendor’s release is visible to them.

They may not call or download any other model, and humans give no research advice. The selection rule is fixed before the campaign starts: the development suite selects the teams submission, and the held-out suite, scored after the campaign, gives the result. Under the campaign protocol, on the held-out suite, the submission closes 97% of the gap between the base and Instruct-2507, where the default starter, at 20.4, closes 30%. The submission scores 46.7 1.3 over two seeds, against 8.7 for the base and 48.0 1.4 for Instruct-2507. Compared with Instruct-2507 on the same items, the submission is 1.3 points lower, and the 95% confidence interval for this difference, paired over items, runs from 4.0 to +1.3: the two models are not distinguishable. All four agents submissions reach this level: they score 45.9 to 47.2, and for each the 95% interval for the difference from Instruct-2507 contains zero. Task profile and comparison with reasoning releases. The team reaches the vendors mean by different route, and the difference repeats on both suites; Figure 10 shows how each task climbs. The submission is above Instruct-2507 on multi-step action (98.9 against 82.4 on development, 78.8 against 65.9 held-out) and code (47.1 against 43.9, and 34.9 against 31.4), above or level on knowledge and instruction following, and below on logic (63.4 against 80.4, and 63.7 against 81.0) and mathematics (37.2 against 42.9, and 29.7 against 42.2). The means are level because multi-step action offsets mathematics and logic: without it, the submission trails Instruct-2507 by 3.7 points on development and by 4.2 on the held-out suite. The agents fine-tune on ALFWorld trajectories, and the gain carries over to the two task types they never saw. The teams models, fine-tuned on reasoning traces, write out their reasoning before they answer, so on logic and mathematics many answers hit the output limit before they end. For the teams submission, 18% of the logic answers and 24% of the mathematics answers are cut off, against 1% and 10% for Instruct-2507 (Appendix D.1). The final measurement (Table 1, bottom) raises the teams means to 67.3 on development and 48.2 on the held-out suite, level with or above Instruct-2507 (66.5 and 47.9; Table 10 gives all four submissions); the paired 95% intervals of the differences, 0.8 to +2.4 and 2.0 to +2.6, contain zero. With longer output limits and sampled decoding, the submissions logic score does not rise (63.4 to 63.0, against 79.5 for Instruct-2507), so truncation is not the whole gap; most of the gap lies in the larger logic puzzles (Appendix D.1). The vendors two reasoning releases score higher still (73.3 and 50.6 for the hybrid release, 80.5 and 63.0 for Thinking-2507), mostly on mathematics, logic, and code: the team reaches the vendors instruct release but not yet its reasoning releases.

sections.title: 4.3 Execution Effectiveness
sections.content: The result above rests on the environment carrying out the agents experiments. This section measures where the agents time, the GPU hours, and the money go, and how the campaign runs over four days. Agent efficiency. The agents spend their time on the research, not on rebuilding the experiment infrastructure, and once session has submitted job, it waits for the result and spends no tokens while waiting (Figure 3b and d; Figure 12 shows each agent separately). Of the roughly 416 agent hours of the campaign, an agent is working (reasoning or running its tool calls) for about 9%. The agents reasoning, in which they read results, analyze them, and decide, takes 15 hours in all (3.6%). Almost all of the agents tool calls run shell commands, most often athanor commands that start jobs and evaluations and read their state; 41 of the 2,611 athanor commands fail, mostly on wrong argument or name. For 87% of the time session waits while its jobs run, until result wakes the agent. turn of agent work lasts 4 seconds at the median, while GRPO job takes 1.6 hours and full evaluation takes 26 minutes (Figure 3c); the GRPO job and the evaluation together make up the feedback delay τfb. The GPUs therefore almost never wait for an agent: less than 1% of the GPU hours pass while an idle GPU waits for its agent. 9 Figure 3 The GPUs stay busy while the agents spend most of their time waiting on jobs. (a) Jobs hold the GPUs for 93% of the GPU hours, shown as three-hour means by phase of the recipe; triangles mark the three nodes the platform took back. (d) 97% of the agents tool calls run Bash, and the athanor commands they run most often start jobs and evaluations, check their state, and delete checkpoints to free disk space (ckpt rm). System efficiency. Jobs hold the GPUs for 93% of the available GPU hours (3,086 of 3,315): of the available hours, 54% go to training (40% go to GRPO alone), 17% go to sampling, almost all for self-distillation, and 22% go to evaluation (Figure 3a). Holding GPU is not computing on it: by the utilization the GPUs report, they compute for about 75% of the available hours. Part of the gap lies inside the training and evaluation stacks: GRPO step waits for the longest rollout of its batch, which leaves GPUs below 10% utilization for 155 GPU hours, and jobs and evaluations spend about 90 GPU hours starting up before their first step. Cost. The campaign has two costs, the GPUs and the agents inference. Claude Code itself counts what each turn costs at public list prices: $1,074 for the whole team. To put the two resources on one scale, we price the GPU time at $3.49 per GPU hour, the median on-demand rental price of GPU of this class across 10 Figure 4 The campaign costs about $11,800, most of it GPU time. The frontier reaches about 50 after $1,100 and about 60 after $2,400, and the submission is first evaluated after about $10,300 (Figure 4b); the last six points, from about 60 to the submissions 66.1, cost about $8,000. Long-horizon reliability. The campaign runs for 104 hours, and the environment absorbs what goes wrong in that time. The platform takes back three of the four nodes during the run, at hours 46, 70, and 94. Each outage lasts 11 to 69 minutes and is added to that agents window; the session resumes on new node from its record, and what is lost is the jobs and evaluations running at that moment, 23 GPU hours of work in all, together with any files kept only on the nodes local disk. Requests rarely fail: 26 of 500 jobs end failed, most of them on errors in the agents own programs, and 2 evaluations end failed. After the campaign every submitted checkpoint, its evaluations, and its lineage are recovered from the record.

sections.title: 5 Trajectory Analysis
sections.content: Because Athanor records every request, result, and checkpoint lineage, the campaign can be traced step by step from the base to the submission. The record of the campaign holds 500 jobs, 255 requested full evaluations (each one seed of the whole development suite; together they score 174 checkpoints), 57 checkpoint fetches between agents, and the transcripts and notes of the four agents. We summarize it as four findings  (Table 2)  : the first describes the recipe the team found, and the other three describe how the team searched. The agents own notes behind each case are in Appendix E.

sections.title: 5.2 Team Progress
sections.content: Ideas and checkpoints move between agents within hours, and the teams best checkpoints combine the training of several agents. Before hour 15.8 the agents read each others files 37 times, but they write no notes for their teammates and fetch no checkpoints. At hour 15.8 the operator tells the agents that the final result counts the teams submission, rule fixed before the start that their documents had not stated; we call 13 this the notice. Within minutes each agent writes its first note for its teammates, and the first checkpoint is fetched from teammate 56 seconds after the notice arrives (Figure 7a). From then on the agents share without further prompting. All four agents are using Agent 3s rollout change within six hours of its first use, and Agent 1s and Agent 4s notes credit Agent 3 for it. Agent 4 takes up Agent 3s extrapolated merge within hours. Agent 2 copies Agent 3s self-distillation programs on the day they are written. Figure 6 The whole search. Each dot is one of the 174 fully evaluated checkpoints, at the hour of its first evaluation and its mean development score, colored by agent; each line joins checkpoint to the evaluated ones it was made from. The teams submission (star) and the 22 evaluated checkpoints it was built from are drawn in full, and their links are dark where the path passes through checkpoint fetched from teammate. The base (16.1) is off the axis. From hour 21, when Agent 4s average of two teammates models (59.95, Trace 5) becomes the best checkpoint, every checkpoint that sets new best score is either merge of models from several agents or was trained from such merge. We link each evaluated checkpoint to the nearest evaluated checkpoints it was made from. This gives 287 links, and for 139 of them the path between the two checkpoints includes checkpoint fetched from teammate (Figure 6; Appendix D.3 lists selection of the exchanges). The agents lineages also grow together over time. Before the notice, no evaluated checkpoint contains any training done by teammate. Of the 32 checkpoints evaluated after hour 84, 28 are built on training by all four agents (Figure 7b). This fits the finding of Park et al. that sharing helps when agents have verifier to tell which teammates results are worth building on [51]; here the development suite plays this role by scoring every checkpoint.

sections.title: 5.3 Recipe Convergence
sections.content: The four agents converge on one recipe early. Within the first hour, each agent chooses AM-Thinking-v1Distilled [1], public corpus of long reasoning traces distilled from stronger model, as the largest source of its fine-tuning data, and each adds few other sources. No agent runs controlled comparison of this corpus against another source. The corpus makes up 7687% of the public-data rows of each agents first mixture (Figure 7c). Their search over data stays narrow: of the 447 datasets in the pool, the agents look at 43 and use 27, and all four use eight of them (Appendix C). The teams attempts to diversify fail. At hour 36, Agent 3 notes that every fine-tuned model of the team is built on that one corpus. To make the merges more diverse, it trains new lineage from the base on other data. The new lineage stays near 55 while the teams best is near 62, and merging it into the main lineage 14 Figure 7 The team starts sharing at the notice and ends up building on all four agents work. By the fourth day, all four agents are refining one model and merging each others variants of it. Anthropics study of multi-agent systems describes the same tendency: agents that share model, harness, and context take very similar actions, so one agents decision becomes the decision of all of them [4].

sections.title: 5.4 Uneven Data Sense
sections.content: The agents inspect their data and act on what they see. Each reads 30 to 70 excerpts of rows from candidate corpora in the first six hours, and later they read their models answers to judge the data behind them. They reject corpora whose reasoning traces exceed the output limit and drop 1,093 instruction rows that the reward function cannot score. They fix deduplication step that had marked every puzzle as duplicate and rebuild puzzle pool that had been mostly small grids. After seeing that model trained on puzzle-solver traces asserts unjustified deductions, they discard those traces. What they rarely do is check whether the answers in the data are correct: one agent notes that some ground-truth answers look like noise, plans filter to remove them, and never runs it (Appendix D.4).

sections.title: 5.5 Why the Gains Slow
sections.content: Figure 1 is the capability curve of autoresearch scaling (Section 2): because jobs hold the GPUs for 93% of the available hours, hours track compute (Figure 4b plots it against cost). The frontier reaches 60 within the first day; the remaining three days add about seven points, the largest share on logic, where the leading checkpoints score rises from 49 to 65 (Figure 10). The findings above suggest why. In the last two days no step on the submissions lineage brings in new training data: the gains of those days come from merging the teams models and from distilling them on their own samples (Section 5.1). All of these models descend from one choice of data made in the first hour, so each merge combines closely related models, and the two lineages trained on other data score lower and are dropped (Section 5.3). 15 Figure 8 Two observations from the record. sections.title: 6 Insights and Discussion
sections.content: Automated scientific discovery of post-training. The record does more than document one result: it turns open questions of post-training into measurements, each tied to the recipe and checkpoints that produced it. If such campaigns run at scale, the first systematic understanding of how post-training shapes model may come from AI agents studying AI rather than from people. In single experiments of this campaign, averaging two equally strong models from different lineages gains two to three points, moving merge further from the base trades knowledge for logic (Figure 8b), and Agent 3s first round of self-distillation adds about one point (Appendix D.6). The agents draw these lessons themselves and write them into their notes as rules for their teammates, such as Agent 4s averaging two EQUAL-strength RL models from different lineages gives +2.7. search of this kind runs such experiments at the rate the compute allows and keeps the evidence behind each conclusion. It can do so only because of what the record keeps. Post-training feedback is slow and noisy (Section 2), so the cause of score has to be recoverable afterwards, and Athanor keeps the answer to every item, repeated evaluations, the lineage of each model, and the teammates work. The rollout change of Section 5.1 came from reading the scored answers, which show that many answers reaching the output limit are caught in repetition loop; record of scores alone would have hidden the cause. Toward broader autoresearch loop. The campaign fixes the suites and excludes teacher models; these boundaries keep the result checkable and also limit what the agents can try. Everything else this campaign rests on was built by people, and each piece could be handed to agents, making the campaign one part of larger loop in which AI improves AI research. The benchmark: agents could construct the evaluation suites for the capabilities they target. The environment: agents could build the next autoresearch environment, for post-training or for other domains, as we build Athanor through the meta loop of Section 3.2. The data: agents could run data flywheel, generating, verifying, and cleaning their own training problems, so that synthetic data becomes an essential part of the search. And the researchers themselves: every campaign leaves complete record of research at scale, with each decision tied to the evidence the agent saw and the result that followed, and such trajectories are training data for models built to do autoresearch. Each step that hands the agents more of the loop needs its own checks, against contamination and against agents that learn to please the evaluator.

sections.title: 7 Related Work
sections.content: Automated post-training. PostTrainBench [55] has an agent post-train small base model for one benchmark on one GPU in ten hours, and Locus [29] extends this setting to parallel, multi-day search; both produce one specialist per benchmark. RSI-Master and RSIGym also train per task, with access to external model APIs and with training and evaluation behind remote services, respectively [16, 47]. RSI Arena [5] runs ten agents as competitors, each post-training the same 30B base model on shared cluster, and ranks their models by human preference. Other benchmarks isolate fine-tuning or reinforcement-learning pipelines [12, 38]. An analysis of PostTrainBench trajectories finds that agents rarely change strategy between consecutive training attempts [39], narrow search like the one we observe. Our setting differs in that team of agents works for days on one generalist checkpoint, without teacher model, and is scored on held-out twin suite. Agents that improve AI systems. Agents now improve the systems around models: their own code and harness [41, 68, 80] and inference engineering [81], up to the production inference service of GLMs own models [77]. All of these work on the layers around the model; our agents change the models weights. Autonomous research and teams of agents. Research agents now carry out experiments over hours to days [26, 43, 48], and benchmarks score machine-learning engineering and research tasks [9, 44, 66, 70]. Work on teams of agents finds that identical agents sharing workspace outperform independent ones when verifier tells them whose progress to build on [51], that agents sharing model, harness, and context behave alike [4], and that single agent can get stuck in an idea basin, small region of ideas it keeps returning to [7]; other systems share work among agents through forum, git history, or co-evolution [13, 53, 82]. Our teams convergence on one corpus resembles an idea basin shared by several agents, measured here on real training compute; Appendix compares Athanor with neighboring systems.

sections.title: 8 Limitations
sections.content: One campaign, one base model, and one agent model. The result comes from one campaign, with one team of four identical agents and one 4B base model. Its four submissions reach the same level, but they share their work and are not independent repeats; repeat would show how much the result varies from campaign to campaign, and campaign without sharing would show how much of it the team adds. We chose 4B base because model of this size can be trained and evaluated many times within one campaign; whether the recipe the team found carries over to larger models or to other model families is untested. The search itself may also change with the agents: agents built on another model may search differently, and team that mixes models may converge less on one recipe than our team of identical agents did. Not yet at the vendors ceiling. The team reaches the vendors instruct release, not its two reasoning releases, which score higher in the final measurement  (Table 1)  . And although the agents call no teacher model, much of the public data they fine-tune on was distilled from stronger models by its publishers [1, 36, 73], so the result shows what agents can build from public resources, not from the base model alone.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: Athanor lets frontier agents run AutoPostTrain end to end. In 104 hours, team of four agents takes Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on six tasks and from 9.2 to 48.2 on held-out twin suite, level with or above the vendors instruct release (66.5 and 47.9), by composing known methods and fixing the problems their own measurements expose. The agents reach this level from public data, for about $12,000 in GPU time and inference. Once the friction of execution is removed, the clearest limit we observe is the diversity of their ideas. This points to future in which anyone who can score the behavior they want automatically, and who has tokens and GPUs, can have agents post-train model for it. We hope that Athanor and our findings will provide foundation for scalable autonomous AI research.

sections.content: This appendix gives the implementation of the three principles of Section 3.3: Execution and protected evaluation implements the first; Workspaces and persistent state and Research record implement the second; and Background jobs and results implements the third. Table 3 makes the roles of Section 3.2 concrete: who decides each matter in campaign and who carries it out. Table 3 Who decides and who carries it out.

sections.title: Carried out by
sections.content: The environments services, which put the request in queue, assign GPUs to the job, and run it The evaluator and the services, as declared Operator commands, each leaving record The operator, through sealed evaluation that the researchers cannot see and are not told about The environment; every analysis in this paper is derived from it Execution and protected evaluation. Each researcher runs in sandbox on its node, with its workspace, scratch disk, the base model, the data pool, and read-only views of its teammates workspaces and results. service outside the sandbox accepts the requests of the athanor command, queues them, binds GPUs, starts and stops jobs, and accounts for GPU time. Evaluation runs outside the sandbox in its own network namespace with frozen copy of the evaluator, and only the scores and scored answers of the development suite are copied back to the researcher. Decontamination also runs outside the sandbox, and the researcher sees only how many rows it removed: row of training dataset is removed if it overlaps benchmark item, either development item or held-out item. To test this, we lowercase the text and remove punctuation and markup. We then list all 13-word sequences in the row and in the item. The row is removed when at least half of the items 13-word sequences also appear in the row. An item shorter than 13 words has no such sequence and is not matched by this rule. Workspaces and persistent state. Everything the record needs is saved to durable storage as it is written: the workspace with its git history, the agents home directory, the journal, the results of every evaluation and job, and every checkpoint saved as an artifact. Large files that the agents leave on the nodes scratch disk, such as training datasets, are not. When the platform reclaims node, the operator starts the session again on new node. Requests that were still running on the lost node are marked as ended in the journal. The outage is added to the research window, and the agent session continues from its saved transcript and notes. Research record. requests journal line is written first, before the request starts anything. If the node fails, the journal still shows what was requested. For every checkpoint the record keeps the job that wrote it, that jobs inputs (datasets, parent checkpoints, and the commit of the workspace when the job started), and the 24 evaluations and artifacts made from it, so the lineage of any checkpoint can be read back to the base model. The researchers notes are ordinary files in their workspaces. Background jobs and results. Each job runs under the service, not under the agents session, so it keeps running when the session ends. When job or an evaluation changes state, its journal line is pushed into the agents session as message. Agents can also add their own watches, such as program that wakes the agent when given line appears in training log.

Post-training systems (Locus, AutoTrainess, AEvolve-Training, the automated alignment researchers (AAR), and RSIGym) also optimize model weights, but none fully targets single generalist model or records in full which checkpoint was made from which. Research systems (AIRA2, CORAL, Arbor, Praxist) keep the state of the research, but they mostly improve program or the solution to one task rather than model weights. sections.title: D Additional Results
sections.content: This appendix gives the evidence behind the main text. Appendix D.1 supports the task profile and the climb of Sections 4.2 and 5.5; Appendix D.2 supports Sections 5.1, 5.3, and 5.4; Appendix D.3 supports Section 5.2; Appendix D.4 supports Section 5.4; Appendix D.5 supports Section 4.3; and Appendix D.6 supports Section 6. D.1 Why the Submission Trails on Logic and Mathematics On logic and mathematics the teams models score below Instruct-2507 (Section 4.2; Figure 10 shows how each task climbs). On logic the cause is the large puzzles, which the models rarely solve; under the campaign protocol this shows as answers cut off at the output limit. We measured this on the development suite, from the record of every answer in two evaluation seeds of the teams submission and of Instruct-2507. Figure 10 How each development task climbs. Multi-step action passes Instruct-2507 by hour 9 and knowledge by hour 21; instruction following comes within point of it by hour 29, and code passes it by hour 32. After the first day, the largest gain is on logic, from 49 to 65, still below Instruct-2507s 80; mathematics stays below throughout. Each panel shows every evaluations score on one task (dots, colored by agent) and, as staircase, the task score of the checkpoint that holds the best development mean so far (the frontier of Figure 1). Dashed and dotted lines are Instruct-2507 and the base under the campaign protocol. The staircase uses single evaluations of the leading checkpoint, so its endpoints are not the submissions multi-seed means of Table 1. On logic, 17.5% of the answers of the teams submission use up the whole 16,384-token output limit before reaching an answer, and each of these answers scores zero. Instruct-2507 has no separate thinking phase and writes shorter answers: only 0.8% are cut off this way. On mathematics the corresponding shares are 24.2% for the teams submission and 9.8% for Instruct-2507. Among the answers that do finish, the teams submission scores 76.4% on logic and 50.1% on mathematics, against 81.0% and 47.2% for Instruct-2507; on logic its finished answers are mostly the smaller puzzles. Cut-off answers concentrate in the large puzzles (Figure 11). The agents noticed this problem themselves, before the operators message at hour 97 that gave each agent its own share of answers cut off  (Table 8)  . This is why their self-distillation keeps only the shortest correct answer to each problem. Four rounds of fine-tuning on the shortest correct samples  (Table 11)  left the share of cut-off logic answers of the four final submissions at 17.518.9%, against 17.4% (87 of 500) for Agent 3s 30 extrapolation before the first round (Trace 4). The reason is that the model is rarely right on the large puzzles, so on those puzzles there are few correct answers to learn from (Figure 11), and few short ones among them (Trace 8). The training pools lean toward small puzzles: Agent 3 keeps only puzzles of at most 16 cells for reinforcement learning (Trace 2). Raising the output limit does not recover these answers. In the final measurement, with an output limit of 32,768 tokens and sampled decoding, the teams submissions logic score changes by less than one point (63.4 to 63.0), and the four final submissions remain 1519 points below Instruct-2507 on logic  (Table 10)  . On mathematics, the answers that finish are at least as accurate as Instruct-2507s, so under the campaign protocol much of the gap shows up as truncation; that the gap persists with the longer limit (38.4 against 44.2) shows that truncation is not all of it, and we have not identified the rest. Figure 11 Logic puzzles by size (campaign protocol). Share of the 500 development logic puzzles that the teams submission and Instruct-2507 solve, grouped by puzzle size. Size is the number of cells (houses attributes). Each team bar stacks the share solved (solid) and the share cut off at the output limit before an answer (hatched). Each score is development mean, and the number of seeds is given in parentheses. Data. The fine-tuning mixtures of Agents 1, 3, and 4, which lead to the submission, differ in their supplementary data: verified competitive code, science questions rewritten as multiple choice, instruction-following data with checkable constraints, chat, and ALFWorld expert trajectories repeated two or three times. Reinforcement learning used 2027 thousand problems per round from public mathematics, code, instruction, and multiple-choice sets and from generated logic grids, with the logic share raised over the rounds. D.4 How the Agents Inspected Data We counted the commands in each agents transcripts that displayed rows of data. These counts are lower bounds: we checked each command that we counted, but other commands may also have displayed rows. In the first six hours each agent displayed about 3070 row excerpts. In the rest of the campaign each displayed 212. Each agent also ran at least six checks on the content of dataset or on how the scorer grades the rows, and several checks that only computed statistics, such as counts and lengths. Besides the catches of Section 5.4, they found answer formats the evaluator would not parse. Correctness was checked less: one agent left suspicious ground truth to filter it did not run, and converter marked solutions verified without comparing them to the expected answer. D.5 The Campaign Agent by Agent Figure 12 shows the campaign of Figure 3 separately for each agent. Each agents GPUs stay busy through the phases of the recipe: fine-tuning in the first hours, then GRPO, and later mostly self-distillation sampling for Agents 2 to 4, with evaluations in between. The agents turns come in bursts as results arrive. The figures top panel shows single evaluations, which run high (Figure 8a); the multi-seed means are in Table 9. 33 D.6 Post-Training Observations Post-training itself remains an open scientific problem: data composition interacts with initialization, objective, stage order, and checkpoint composition. The record of the campaign holds such interactions as measured lineages. Each of the following is single observation. When two reinforcement-learning models of equal strength (near 57) from different lineages are averaged, the average scores about 2.7 points higher than the better parent (Trace 5). When strong model is averaged with weaker ones, the average scores no higher than the strong model alone (an observation in Agent 4s notes; Trace 5). When Agent 3 moves merged model further from the base, its logic score rises as the factor grows from 1.0 to 1.2 (56.4, 59.6, 63.0 at factors 1.0, 1.1, 1.2), and its knowledge score falls once the factor passes 1.1 (66.8, 65.7, 63.8 at factors 1.1, 1.2, 1.3); the best factor therefore depends on which task matters more (Figure 8b). Self-distillation (training model on its own sampled answers) raises its score by 1.0 point (three seeds) in its first round; later rounds change it by at most 0.2  (Table 11)  . Fine-tuning different merge on the same samples does not help on its own: the result scores 65.3, against 65.5 for the merge before, although averaging it with Agent 3s self-distilled model gives 65.9  (Table 11)  .

sections.title: E Research Trajectories
sections.content: This appendix shows the agents own work behind the findings of Section 5. Each quote is copied from an agents notes file or from the file it writes for its teammates; r1r4 in the quotes are Agents 14, and an ellipsis marks an omission. In the agents shorthand, dev6 is the development suite; zebra, mmlu (or mcq), ifeval, and alfworld are its logic, knowledge, instruction-following, and multi-step action tasks; soup is an average of checkpoints; diag is diagnostic evaluation on some of the tasks; RFT (also expert iteration) is rejection-sampling fine-tuning, the self-distillation of Section 5.1; RESP is the length limit of one answer in training rollout; names such as s3Lm or soup-e are the agents checkpoint names; official is Instruct-2507; and the other abbreviations (T, sN, val) are as in Section 5.1. E.1 Complete Agent Turn The research episode shown in Section 5.1 turns on one step, in which Agent 3 replaces sampled rollouts with mix of sampled and greedy ones. Of the 55 cut-off logic answers, 33 are loops. 2. Find where the trainer sets its sampling. The agent runs four commands to read three pieces of code: the installed trainers code for rollouts (the files single_turn_agent_loop.py and agent_loop.py of verl), and starter that already replaces the rollout loop for ALFWorld. It looks for two things: where the trainer passes the sampling temperature to the model, and how the trainer registers custom rollout loop. 3. Write the new rollout loop. It subclasses the trainers loop, with its reason in the docstring. $ cat > /workspace/rl/greedy_mix_loop.py <<'EOF' """Single-turn agent loop that decodes share of the training rollouts greedily. dev6 decodes five of its six tasks greedily, and the SFT model's greedy answers loop where its sampled ones (T 0.8) do not: in grpo1's first 25 steps, 2-7 % of the sampled rollouts cut at RESP were repetition loops, against 55-100 % of the greedy validation answers cut there, and 25 steps of GRPO on sampled rollouts left greedy truncation where it was.
